claim: COVID-19 is caused by the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2).
source: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is caused by the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and can affect multiple organs, among which is the circulatory system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the causative agent of COVID-19.

claim: COVID-19 can affect multiple organs, including the circulatory system.
source: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is caused by the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and can affect multiple organs, among which is the circulatory system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COVID-19's multi-organ effects.

claim: Inflammation and mortality risk markers were previously detected in COVID-19 plasma and red blood cells metabolic and proteomic profiles.
source: Inflammation and mortality risk markers were previously detected in COVID-19 plasma and red blood cells (RBCs) metabolic and proteomic profiles.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Biophysical properties such as deformability were found to be changed during COVID-19 infection.
source: Additionally, biophysical properties, such as deformability, were found to be changed during the infection.
evidence: This references prior findings about RBC deformability changes in COVID-19.

claim: Strong flow and RBC shape impairment is found in COVID-19 samples.
source: We find strong flow and RBC shape impairment in COVID-19 samples and demonstrate that such changes are reversible upon suspension of COVID-19 RBCs in healthy plasma.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's microfluidic experiments.

claim: RBC shape changes in COVID-19 are reversible upon suspension of COVID-19 RBCs in healthy plasma.
source: We find strong flow and RBC shape impairment in COVID-19 samples and demonstrate that such changes are reversible upon suspension of COVID-19 RBCs in healthy plasma.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from plasma exchange experiments.

claim: Healthy RBCs resemble COVID-19 RBCs when suspended in COVID-19 plasma.
source: Vice versa, healthy RBCs resemble COVID-19 RBCs when suspended in COVID-19 plasma.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from plasma exchange experiments.

claim: Proteomics and metabolomics analyses detect the effect of plasma exchanges on both plasma and RBCs.
source: Proteomics and metabolomics analyses allow us to detect the effect of plasma exchanges on both plasma and RBCs and demonstrate a new role of RBCs in maintaining plasma equilibria at the expense of their flow properties.
evidence: This is based on the omics analyses performed in the study.

claim: RBCs have a new role in maintaining plasma equilibria at the expense of their flow properties.
source: Proteomics and metabolomics analyses allow us to detect the effect of plasma exchanges on both plasma and RBCs and demonstrate a new role of RBCs in maintaining plasma equilibria at the expense of their flow properties.
evidence: This is a novel interpretation derived from the combined microfluidic and omics data.

claim: Infection with SARS-CoV-2 can lead to the development of COVID-19.
source: Infection with the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) can lead to the development of the Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claim: The pathophysiology of COVID-19 is characterized by respiratory manifestations.
source: The pathophysiology of COVID-19 is characterized by respiratory manifestations but also involves increased inflammatory responses (Mehta et al., 2020), alterations in the number and phenotype of blood cells (Mann et al., 2020; Kubánková et al., 2021), microthrombotic complications, and vascular occlusions that can be fatal (Tang et al., 2020; Varatharajah and Rajah, 2020; Della Rocca et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge about COVID-19 pathophysiology.

claim: COVID-19 involves increased inflammatory responses.
source: The pathophysiology of COVID-19 is characterized by respiratory manifestations but also involves increased inflammatory responses (Mehta et al., 2020), alterations in the number and phenotype of blood cells (Mann et al., 2020; Kubánková et al., 2021), microthrombotic complications, and vascular occlusions that can be fatal (Tang et al., 2020; Varatharajah and Rajah, 2020; Della Rocca et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2020.

claim: COVID-19 involves alterations in the number and phenotype of blood cells.
source: The pathophysiology of COVID-19 is characterized by respiratory manifestations but also involves increased inflammatory responses (Mehta et al., 2020), alterations in the number and phenotype of blood cells (Mann et al., 2020; Kubánková et al., 2021), microthrombotic complications, and vascular occlusions that can be fatal (Tang et al., 2020; Varatharajah and Rajah, 2020; Della Rocca et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mann et al., 2020 and Kubánková et al., 2021.

claim: COVID-19 involves microthrombotic complications and vascular occlusions that can be fatal.
source: The pathophysiology of COVID-19 is characterized by respiratory manifestations but also involves increased inflammatory responses (Mehta et al., 2020), alterations in the number and phenotype of blood cells (Mann et al., 2020; Kubánková et al., 2021), microthrombotic complications, and vascular occlusions that can be fatal (Tang et al., 2020; Varatharajah and Rajah, 2020; Della Rocca et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2020; Varatharajah and Rajah, 2020; Della Rocca et al., 2021.

claim: RBCs in COVID-19 exhibit structural protein damage.
source: In these changes, red blood cells (RBCs) were found to exhibit structural protein damage, membrane lipid remodeling (Thomas et al., 2020a), dysregulation in serum levels of coagulation factors (D'Alessandro et al., 2020), as well as altered physical and rheological properties, such as shape, size, and deformability (Kubánková et al., 2021; Renoux et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2020a.

claim: RBCs in COVID-19 exhibit membrane lipid remodeling.
source: In these changes, red blood cells (RBCs) were found to exhibit structural protein damage, membrane lipid remodeling (Thomas et al., 2020a), dysregulation in serum levels of coagulation factors (D'Alessandro et al., 2020), as well as altered physical and rheological properties, such as shape, size, and deformability (Kubánková et al., 2021; Renoux et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2020a.

claim: COVID-19 involves dysregulation in serum levels of coagulation factors.
source: In these changes, red blood cells (RBCs) were found to exhibit structural protein damage, membrane lipid remodeling (Thomas et al., 2020a), dysregulation in serum levels of coagulation factors (D'Alessandro et al., 2020), as well as altered physical and rheological properties, such as shape, size, and deformability (Kubánková et al., 2021; Renoux et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to D'Alessandro et al., 2020.

claim: RBCs in COVID-19 exhibit altered physical and rheological properties, such as shape, size, and deformability.
source: In these changes, red blood cells (RBCs) were found to exhibit structural protein damage, membrane lipid remodeling (Thomas et al., 2020a), dysregulation in serum levels of coagulation factors (D'Alessandro et al., 2020), as well as altered physical and rheological properties, such as shape, size, and deformability (Kubánková et al., 2021; Renoux et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kubánková et al., 2021 and Renoux et al., 2021.

claim: Changes in RBC mechanical properties can dramatically alter their morphology.
source: Changes in RBC mechanical properties, such as its bending rigidity and cytoplasm viscosity, can dramatically alter their morphology, reduce microvascular perfusion, damage the endothelial cells lining the blood vessel walls, and impact flow behavior and hemorheology of blood in the circulatory system, eventually affecting gas transport efficiency (Lipowsky, 2005; Matthews et al., 2015; Lanotte et al., 2016; Di Carlo, 2012; Piety et al., 2021; Caruso et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations about RBC mechanics and flow.

claim: Changes in RBC mechanical properties can reduce microvascular perfusion.
source: Changes in RBC mechanical properties, such as its bending rigidity and cytoplasm viscosity, can dramatically alter their morphology, reduce microvascular perfusion, damage the endothelial cells lining the blood vessel walls, and impact flow behavior and hemorheology of blood in the circulatory system, eventually affecting gas transport efficiency (Lipowsky, 2005; Matthews et al., 2015; Lanotte et al., 2016; Di Carlo, 2012; Piety et al., 2021; Caruso et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations about RBC mechanics and flow.

claim: Changes in RBC mechanical properties can damage the endothelial cells lining the blood vessel walls.
source: Changes in RBC mechanical properties, such as its bending rigidity and cytoplasm viscosity, can dramatically alter their morphology, reduce microvascular perfusion, damage the endothelial cells lining the blood vessel walls, and impact flow behavior and hemorheology of blood in the circulatory system, eventually affecting gas transport efficiency (Lipowsky, 2005; Matthews et al., 2015; Lanotte et al., 2016; Di Carlo, 2012; Piety et al., 2021; Caruso et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations about RBC mechanics and flow.

claim: Changes in RBC mechanical properties can impact flow behavior and hemorheology of blood in the circulatory system.
source: Changes in RBC mechanical properties, such as its bending rigidity and cytoplasm viscosity, can dramatically alter their morphology, reduce microvascular perfusion, damage the endothelial cells lining the blood vessel walls, and impact flow behavior and hemorheology of blood in the circulatory system, eventually affecting gas transport efficiency (Lipowsky, 2005; Matthews et al., 2015; Lanotte et al., 2016; Di Carlo, 2012; Piety et al., 2021; Caruso et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations about RBC mechanics and flow.

claim: Changes in RBC mechanical properties can affect gas transport efficiency.
source: Changes in RBC mechanical properties, such as its bending rigidity and cytoplasm viscosity, can dramatically alter their morphology, reduce microvascular perfusion, damage the endothelial cells lining the blood vessel walls, and impact flow behavior and hemorheology of blood in the circulatory system, eventually affecting gas transport efficiency (Lipowsky, 2005; Matthews et al., 2015; Lanotte et al., 2016; Di Carlo, 2012; Piety et al., 2021; Caruso et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations about RBC mechanics and flow.

claim: The origin of pathological changes of COVID-19 RBCs and their impact on blood flow remains poorly understood.
source: However, the origin of pathological changes of COVID-19 RBCs and their impact on blood flow remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: RBC flow properties are particularly relevant in the microvasculature, especially in capillaries, where gas exchanges and microthrombotic events occur.
source: RBC flow properties are particularly relevant in the microvasculature, especially in capillaries, where gas exchanges and microthrombotic events occur.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBC function in the microvasculature.

claim: Kubánková et al., 2021 studied the microfluidic flow of RBCs from COVID-19 patients suspended in PBS solution in a channel with a cross-section of 20 × 20 µm2, resulting in cell velocities up to 30 cm s-1.
source: Recently, Kubánková et al., 2021 studied the microfluidic flow of RBCs from COVID-19 patients suspended a in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution in a channel with a cross-section of 20 × 20 µm2, resulting in cell velocities up to 30 cm s-1.
evidence: This is a description of prior work by Kubánková et al., 2021.

claim: At high velocities in microfluidic channels, RBC deformability in COVID-19 patients is heterogeneous, with most RBCs being strongly elongated but some exhibiting circular, less deformable shapes compared with healthy controls.
source: At such high velocities, RBC deformability turned out to be heterogeneous, with most of the RBCs being strongly elongated in the flow direction but some exhibiting circular, less deformable shapes compared with healthy controls.
evidence: This describes findings from Kubánková et al., 2021.

claim: Human capillaries have diameters similar to RBC size (about 10 µm).
source: In human capillaries, which have diameters similar to RBC size (about 10 µm), confined flows confer to RBCs characteristic shapes that depend on the cell velocity and the surrounding medium (Guckenberger et al., 2018; Recktenwald et al., 2022a; Recktenwald et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about capillary dimensions.

claim: Confined flows in capillaries confer to RBCs characteristic shapes that depend on the cell velocity and the surrounding medium.
source: In human capillaries, which have diameters similar to RBC size (about 10 µm), confined flows confer to RBCs characteristic shapes that depend on the cell velocity and the surrounding medium (Guckenberger et al., 2018; Recktenwald et al., 2022a; Recktenwald et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on RBC shapes in confined flow.

claim: Artificial neural networks were previously used to analyze RBC shapes at high detail.
source: We previously used a microfluidic setup with channel dimensions similar to the RBC size and analyzed RBC shapes at high detail by means of artificial neural networks (Kihm et al., 2018) in a velocity range that resembles microvascular in vivo flow.
evidence: This references prior work by the authors using neural networks for RBC analysis.

claim: Flow properties of RBCs depend on biophysical cell features that are influenced by biochemical characteristics.
source: Flow properties of RBCs depend on biophysical cell features that are influenced by biochemical characteristics.
evidence: This is a general principle about RBC biophysics and biochemistry.

claim: RBC flow impairment is observed in COVID-19 plasma.
source: We observe RBC flow impairment in COVID-19 plasma and a full recovery upon suspension in healthy plasma.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the microfluidic experiments.

claim: RBCs show full recovery of flow properties upon suspension in healthy plasma.
source: We observe RBC flow impairment in COVID-19 plasma and a full recovery upon suspension in healthy plasma.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the microfluidic experiments.

claim: Proteomics and metabolomics analyses highlight a mutual influence between RBCs and plasma.
source: To better understand these effects, we additionally characterize both RBCs and plasma content by proteomics and metabolomics analyses, highlighting a mutual influence between RBCs and plasma and discovering a new role of RBCs in influencing plasma homeostasis in COVID-19.
evidence: This is based on the omics analyses performed in the study.

claim: RBCs have a new role in influencing plasma homeostasis in COVID-19.
source: To better understand these effects, we additionally characterize both RBCs and plasma content by proteomics and metabolomics analyses, highlighting a mutual influence between RBCs and plasma and discovering a new role of RBCs in influencing plasma homeostasis in COVID-19.
evidence: This is a novel finding derived from the combined omics and microfluidic data.

claim: Healthy controls form biconcave RBCs that organize into rouleaux in stasis.
source: While healthy controls (CinC) form biconcave RBCs that organize into rouleaux, sphero-echinocytes for COVID-19 patients in autologous plasma (PinP) are found in stasis and highlight impaired RBC clustering (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in microscopy images of RBCs in stasis.

claim: Sphero-echinocytes are found in COVID-19 patients in autologous plasma in stasis.
source: While healthy controls (CinC) form biconcave RBCs that organize into rouleaux, sphero-echinocytes for COVID-19 patients in autologous plasma (PinP) are found in stasis and highlight impaired RBC clustering (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in microscopy images of RBCs in stasis.

claim: COVID-19 patients show impaired RBC clustering in autologous plasma.
source: While healthy controls (CinC) form biconcave RBCs that organize into rouleaux, sphero-echinocytes for COVID-19 patients in autologous plasma (PinP) are found in stasis and highlight impaired RBC clustering (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in microscopy images and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Upon plasma exchange with control plasma, COVID-19 RBC shapes in stasis revert to biconcave disks and are able to aggregate into rouleaux.
source: However, upon plasma exchange (PinC), COVID-19 RBC shapes in stasis revert to biconcave disks and are able to aggregate into rouleaux.
evidence: This is observed in microscopy images after plasma exchange.

claim: Control cells suspended in patient plasma show the opposite trend to patient cells in control plasma.
source: The opposite trend is observed for control cells suspended in patient plasma (CinP).
evidence: This is observed in the microscopy and quantification data.

claim: The ratio of RBCs in clusters over the total number of RBCs quantifies the differences between CinC and PinP.
source: The ratio of RBCs in clusters over the total number of RBCs quantifies the differences between CinC and PinP and shows the recovery of patient RBCs for PinC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, left panel).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from image analysis.

claim: The number of RBCs per cluster in CinC is about twice the number of PinP.
source: The number of RBCs per cluster in CinC is about twice the number of PinP.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: Patient cell shape and rouleaux formation recovery in control plasma (PinC) results in no significant differences with control RBCs (CinC).
source: Notably, patient cell shape and rouleaux formation recovery in control plasma (PinC) results in no significant differences with control RBCs (CinC) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the clustering data.

claim: Healthy RBCs predominantly deform into centered croissants and off-centered slipper shapes in confined flows.
source: In confined flows with dimensions on the same order of magnitude as the diameter of RBCs, healthy RBCs predominantly deform into centered croissants and off-centered slipper shapes (Figure 1C), depending on the cell velocity.
evidence: This is observed in the microfluidic flow experiments.

claim: RBCs of COVID-19 patients exhibit pathological croissant and slipper shapes that display pronounced spicules on the membrane.
source: RBCs of COVID-19 patients additionally exhibit complementary pathological croissant and slipper shapes that resemble their corresponding healthy classes but display pronounced spicules on the membrane (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is observed in the microfluidic flow experiments and images.

claim: COVID-19 patients show sphero-echinocytes in flow, which are irreversible transformations of RBCs that can occur upon ATP depletion, high pH, or exposure to anionic detergents.
source: Further, COVID-19 patients show sphero-echinocytes in flow, known as irreversible transformations of RBCs that can occur upon ATP depletion, high pH, or exposure to anionic detergents (Lim, 2009; Bernhardt and Ellory, 2013; Figure 1D).
evidence: The observation is from the study's data, while the characterization of sphero-echinocytes is from cited literature.

claim: The RBC shape phase diagram describes the frequency of occurrence for RBC morphologies as a function of cell velocity.
source: The so-called RBC shape phase diagram (Kihm et al., 2018; Guckenberger et al., 2018; Recktenwald et al., 2022a; Recktenwald et al., 2022b) describes the frequency of occurrence for RBC morphologies as a function of cell velocity.
evidence: This is a methodological concept from prior work.

claim: Croissant- and slipper-like shapes emerge for control samples in autologous plasma (CinC).
source: While croissant- and slipper-like shapes emerge for control samples in autologous plasma (CinC), corresponding pathological shapes and sphero-echinocytes dominate for patient RBCs in autologous plasma (PinP) (Figure 1E, top graphs).
evidence: This is shown in the shape phase diagrams from the microfluidic experiments.

claim: Pathological shapes and sphero-echinocytes dominate for patient RBCs in autologous plasma (PinP).
source: While croissant- and slipper-like shapes emerge for control samples in autologous plasma (CinC), corresponding pathological shapes and sphero-echinocytes dominate for patient RBCs in autologous plasma (PinP) (Figure 1E, top graphs).
evidence: This is shown in the shape phase diagrams from the microfluidic experiments.

claim: Upon plasma exchange with healthy control plasma, patient RBCs (PinC) show a shape reversal, exhibiting a phase diagram similar to healthy controls.
source: However, upon plasma exchange with healthy control plasma, patient RBCs (PinC) show a shape reversal, exhibiting a phase diagram similar to healthy controls.
evidence: This is shown in the shape phase diagrams after plasma exchange.

claim: Control RBCs in allogeneic exchanged COVID-19 plasma (CinP) result in a drastic RBC shape deterioration.
source: In contrast, control RBCs in allogeneic exchanged COVID-19 plasma (CinP) result in a drastic RBC shape deterioration (Figure 1E, bottom graphs).
evidence: This is shown in the shape phase diagrams after plasma exchange.

claim: The fraction of pathological cells is considerably small for healthy controls (CinC).
source: While this fraction is considerably small for healthy controls (CinC), COVID-19 patients (PinP) show pathological fractions of up to one in autologous plasma (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is quantified from the microfluidic flow analysis.

claim: COVID-19 patients (PinP) show pathological fractions of up to one in autologous plasma.
source: While this fraction is considerably small for healthy controls (CinC), COVID-19 patients (PinP) show pathological fractions of up to one in autologous plasma (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is quantified from the microfluidic flow analysis.

claim: Upon plasma exchange (PinC), all patients exhibit a decrease in the pathological fraction.
source: Upon plasma exchange (PinC), all patients exhibit a decrease in the pathological fraction, hence a reduction in the number of pathological RBC shapes.
evidence: This is quantified from the microfluidic flow analysis after plasma exchange.

claim: Healthy RBCs suspended in COVID-19 plasma (CinP) show an increase in pathological shapes compared to their control condition (CinC).
source: In contrast, healthy RBCs suspended in COVID-19 plasma (CinP) show an increase in pathological shapes compared to their control condition (CinC).
evidence: This is quantified from the microfluidic flow analysis after plasma exchange.

claim: Suspension in allogeneic plasma results in a reduction of sphero-echinocytes for all patients.
source: Similarly, suspension in allogeneic plasma results in a reduction of sphero-echinocytes for all patients, while an increase is observed for the controls in COVID-19 plasma (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is quantified from the microfluidic flow analysis after plasma exchange.

claim: An increase in sphero-echinocytes is observed for controls in COVID-19 plasma.
source: Similarly, suspension in allogeneic plasma results in a reduction of sphero-echinocytes for all patients, while an increase is observed for the controls in COVID-19 plasma (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is quantified from the microfluidic flow analysis after plasma exchange.

claim: The large number of sphero-echinocytes in RBCs suspended in COVID-19 plasma leads to a decrease of the 2D projection area compared to healthy shapes.
source: The pronounced number of sphero-echinocytes in RBCs suspended in COVID-19 plasma leads to a decrease of the 2D projection area in the x-y-plane compared to healthy shapes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is measured from the microfluidic flow analysis.

claim: The large number of sphero-echinocytes and impaired deformability of pathological RBCs in COVID-19 plasma hinders the formation of stable slipper-shaped RBCs at high velocities.
source: The large number of sphero-echinocytes and the impaired deformability of pathological RBCs in COVID-19 plasma (PinP and CinP) hinders the formation of stable slipper-shaped RBCs at high velocities.
evidence: This is inferred from the shape analysis and flow behavior observations.

claim: Impaired deformability causes pronounced deviations from the single-cell flow behavior of healthy cells, as expressed by the deviation in the equilibrium position in y-direction.
source: This causes pronounced deviations from the single-cell flow behavior of healthy cells, as expressed by the deviation in the equilibrium position in y-direction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is measured from the microfluidic flow analysis.

claim: Control plasma content results in higher levels of albumin (ALB), transferrin (TF), and gelsolin (GSN) compared to patient plasma.
source: Control plasma content results in higher levels of albumin (ALB), transferrin (TF), and gelsolin (GSN).
evidence: This is from the proteomics analysis comparing control and patient plasma.

claim: Decreased levels of albumin, transferrin, and gelsolin are associated with hypercoagulability, higher inflammatory state, and severity in COVID-19, respectively.
source: Decreased levels of such proteins are associated with hypercoagulability, higher inflammatory state, and severity in COVID-19, respectively (Violi et al., 2021; Claise et al., 2022; Messner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Patient plasma is associated with an increase in inflammation and coagulation markers, such as complement cascade proteins, SERPINA1, SERPINA3, SERPINA G1, and C-reactive protein (CRP).
source: On the contrary, patient plasma is associated with an increase in inflammation and coagulation markers, such as complement cascade proteins (such as C2, C3, C5, C7, C9), SERPINA1, SERPINA3, and SERPINA G1 and C-reactive protein (CRP).
evidence: This is from the proteomics analysis of patient plasma.

claim: Patient plasma becomes comparable to control plasma content upon suspension with control RBCs (CinP).
source: Specifically, patient plasma becomes comparable to control plasma content upon suspension with control RBCs (CinP), while the opposite effect occurs in control plasma suspended with patient RBCs (PinC) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is from the proteomics and metabolomics analysis after plasma exchange.

claim: The opposite effect occurs in control plasma suspended with patient RBCs (PinC).
source: Specifically, patient plasma becomes comparable to control plasma content upon suspension with control RBCs (CinP), while the opposite effect occurs in control plasma suspended with patient RBCs (PinC) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is from the proteomics and metabolomics analysis after plasma exchange.

claim: RBCs strongly influence plasma content.
source: This shows a strong influence of RBCs on plasma content and highlights the establishment of an equilibrium between RBCs and plasma.
evidence: This is inferred from the omics data showing changes in plasma composition after RBC suspension.

claim: An equilibrium is established between RBCs and plasma.
source: This shows a strong influence of RBCs on plasma content and highlights the establishment of an equilibrium between RBCs and plasma.
evidence: This is inferred from the omics data showing bidirectional changes.

claim: The fraction of pathological RBC shapes and sphero-echinocyte percentage are comparable in RBCs suspended in patient plasma, although plasma content is different.
source: Notably, the fraction of pathological RBC shapes and sphero-echinocyte percentage are comparable in RBCs suspended in patient plasma, although plasma content is different.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the microfluidic and omics data.

claim: RBC influence on plasma content occurs at the expense of RBC morphology, which in turn affects RBC flow properties.
source: This means that RBC influence on plasma content occurs at the expense of RBC morphology, which in turn, affects RBC flow properties.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observation of plasma changes and RBC morphological impairment.

claim: The impairment of RBC shape is not directly caused by a specific plasma component but may derive from a complex interaction between plasma and RBCs.
source: Additionally, these results show that the impairment of RBC shape is not directly caused by a specific plasma component but may derive from a complex interaction between plasma and RBCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple plasma components change together.

claim: Principal component analysis highlights four distinct groups in plasma content.
source: In agreement with the data in the heat map, principal component analysis (PCA) highlights four distinct groups, showing that plasma contents of the groups CinP and CinC result in neighboring clusters, while PinC and PinP clusters strongly overlap (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from the PCA analysis of the omics data.

claim: Plasma contents of the groups CinP and CinC result in neighboring clusters in PCA.
source: In agreement with the data in the heat map, principal component analysis (PCA) highlights four distinct groups, showing that plasma contents of the groups CinP and CinC result in neighboring clusters, while PinC and PinP clusters strongly overlap (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from the PCA analysis of the omics data.

claim: PinC and PinP clusters strongly overlap in PCA.
source: In agreement with the data in the heat map, principal component analysis (PCA) highlights four distinct groups, showing that plasma contents of the groups CinP and CinC result in neighboring clusters, while PinC and PinP clusters strongly overlap (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is from the PCA analysis of the omics data.

claim: Tryptophan metabolism is altered in COVID-19 plasma, resulting in decreased anthranilate and indole acetaldehyde and increased kynurenine in patients.
source: As previously described (Thomas et al., 2020b), tryptophan metabolism is altered in COVID-19 plasma, resulting in decreased anthranilate and indole acetaldehyde and increased kynurenine in patients, which is associated with a higher mortality risk (Thomas et al., 2020b; Mangge et al., 2021; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and confirmed in the current study's data.

claim: Altered tryptophan metabolism in COVID-19 is associated with a higher mortality risk.
source: As previously described (Thomas et al., 2020b), tryptophan metabolism is altered in COVID-19 plasma, resulting in decreased anthranilate and indole acetaldehyde and increased kynurenine in patients, which is associated with a higher mortality risk (Thomas et al., 2020b; Mangge et al., 2021; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Plasma kynurenine significantly increases upon exposure of patient RBCs in control plasma (PinC) compared to control conditions (CinC).
source: Compared to control conditions (CinC), plasma kynurenine significantly increases upon exposure of patient RBCs in control plasma (PinC).
evidence: This is from the metabolomics analysis after plasma exchange.

claim: Tryptophan levels are significantly lower in patient plasma (PinP) compared to controls (CinC).
source: Tryptophan levels are significantly lower in patient plasma (PinP) compared to controls (CinC), while they significantly increase for control RBCs in patient plasma (CinP).
evidence: This is from the metabolomics analysis.

claim: Tryptophan levels significantly increase for control RBCs in patient plasma (CinP).
source: Tryptophan levels are significantly lower in patient plasma (PinP) compared to controls (CinC), while they significantly increase for control RBCs in patient plasma (CinP).
evidence: This is from the metabolomics analysis after plasma exchange.

claim: Plasma anthranilate levels and tryptophan/kynurenine (Trp/Kyn) ratio significantly differ in the groups with control RBCs (CinC and CinP) compared to patients groups (PinC and PinP).
source: Plasma anthranilate levels and tryptophan/kynurenine (Trp/Kyn) ratio significantly differ in the groups with control RBCs (CinC and CinP) compared to patients groups (PinC and PinP).
evidence: This is from the metabolomics analysis.

claim: RBCs play a role in buffering kynurenine content and related metabolites, thus potentially protecting from an increased risk for mortality in COVID-19 patients.
source: These data suggest a role of RBCs in buffering kynurenine content and related metabolites, thus potentially protecting from an increased risk for mortality in COVID-19 patients (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in kynurenine pathway metabolites after plasma exchange.

claim: Most proteins and metabolites in RBCs that differ between groups involve plasma proteins such as albumin, fibrinogen, gelsolin, transferrin, serpins, and immunoglobulin variables.
source: Most of them involve plasma proteins, such as albumin (ALB), fibrinogen (FGA and FGB), gelsolin (GSN), transferrin (TF), serpins (SERPINA1, SEPRINC1), and immunoglobulin variables (IGHV439, IGHG2, IGKC) (Figure 4A), which result significantly different in the respective control and patient plasma samples.
evidence: This is from the proteomics analysis of RBCs.

claim: Some characteristics of RBCs are maintained only when they are suspended in autologous plasma.
source: Additionally, two clusters indicate that some characteristics of RBCs are maintained only when they are suspended in autologous plasma.
evidence: This is inferred from the clustering analysis of RBC omics data.

claim: Control RBCs (CinC) show higher levels of pantothenol, which is known to have antiseptic properties.
source: Control RBCs (CinC) show higher levels of pantothenol, which is known to have antiseptic properties (Saliba et al., 2005), adenosine and hydroxyglutarate that were found decreased in hypoxia (Nemkov et al., 2018), and formyl-kynurenine, probably buffering plasma kynurenine (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from the metabolomics analysis of RBCs, with the property of pantothenol cited from literature.

claim: Control RBCs show higher levels of adenosine and hydroxyglutarate that were found decreased in hypoxia.
source: Control RBCs (CinC) show higher levels of pantothenol, which is known to have antiseptic properties (Saliba et al., 2005), adenosine and hydroxyglutarate that were found decreased in hypoxia (Nemkov et al., 2018), and formyl-kynurenine, probably buffering plasma kynurenine (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from the metabolomics analysis of RBCs, with the hypoxia association cited from literature.

claim: Control RBCs show higher levels of formyl-kynurenine, probably buffering plasma kynurenine.
source: Control RBCs (CinC) show higher levels of pantothenol, which is known to have antiseptic properties (Saliba et al., 2005), adenosine and hydroxyglutarate that were found decreased in hypoxia (Nemkov et al., 2018), and formyl-kynurenine, probably buffering plasma kynurenine (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from the metabolomics analysis with an inference about the buffering role.

claim: The most abundant proteins in patient RBCs (PinP) are linked to cellular responses to stress.
source: In contrast, the most abundant proteins in patient RBCs (PinP) are linked to cellular responses to stress (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), involving ubiquitination and protein degradation by the proteasome, which may be related to a higher oxidative stress.
evidence: This is from the proteomics analysis and STRING pathway analysis.

claim: Patient RBCs show proteins involved in ubiquitination and protein degradation by the proteasome, which may be related to higher oxidative stress.
source: In contrast, the most abundant proteins in patient RBCs (PinP) are linked to cellular responses to stress (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), involving ubiquitination and protein degradation by the proteasome, which may be related to a higher oxidative stress.
evidence: This is from the proteomics analysis with an inference about oxidative stress.

claim: Increasing levels of guanidinoacetate, ornithine, urate, and L-citrulline in patient RBCs indicate higher catabolism of arginine.
source: Increasing levels of guanidinoacetate, ornithine, urate, and L-citrulline indicate higher catabolism of arginine.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolomics data showing increased arginine catabolism products.

claim: RBCs must adapt their metabolism and protein content when they influence plasma metabolites and protein abundance.
source: Since RBCs influence plasma metabolites and protein abundance, they must necessarily adapt their metabolism and protein content.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observed bidirectional changes.

claim: An effect occurs when RBCs are suspended in allogeneic plasma (CinP and PinC), resulting in changed levels of plasma proteins and immunoglobulin variables.
source: Indeed, an effect occurs when RBCs are suspended in allogeneic plasma (CinP and PinC), resulting in changed levels of plasma proteins (ALB, FGA, FGB, GSN, TF, SERPINA1, SERPINC1) and immunoglobulin variables (IGHV439, IGHG2, IGKC) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is from the proteomics analysis of RBCs after plasma exchange.

claim: RBCs have acute ability to equilibrate their protein levels when coming in contact with new plasma.
source: These data indicate RBC acute ability to equilibrate their protein levels when coming in contact with new plasma, since the first cluster is comparable between CinC and PinP and between CinP and PinC (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the clustering patterns in the omics data.

claim: The changes in RBC metabolism and protein content that occur upon suspension with allogeneic plasma do not reflect RBC morphological changes.
source: However, the changes in RBC metabolism and protein content that occur upon suspension with allogeneic plasma do not reflect RBC morphological changes, since PinP samples exhibit many more pathological RBC shapes than PinC samples.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the omics and microfluidic data.

claim: The fraction of pathological cells correlates with hypoxanthine, ectoine, and nicotinamide in plasma.
source: The fraction of pathological cells also correlates to hypoxanthine, ectoine, and nicotinamide.
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: TF levels negatively correlate with sphero-echinocyte percentage and fraction of pathological RBC shapes.
source: TF levels negatively correlate to sphero-echinocyte percentage and fraction of pathological RBC shapes.
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: TF was previously reported to decrease during COVID-19 infection.
source: TF was previously reported to decrease during COVID-19 infection (Claise et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Claise et al., 2022.

claim: The levels of arginine and tyrosine were previously reported to negatively correlate with disease severity, as gleaned by the levels of the inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 (IL-6).
source: Similarly, the levels of arginine and tyrosine were previously reported to negatively correlate with disease severity, as gleaned by the levels of the inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6 (IL-6) (Thomas et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2020b.

claim: Decreases are observed in the levels of sulfur-containing amino acids, thiocysteine, 3-sufinoalanine, and cystine, a marker of redox homeostasis.
source: Analogously, decreases are observed in the levels of sulfur-containing amino acids, thiocysteine, 3-sufinoalanine, and cystine, a marker of redox homeostasis.
evidence: This is from the metabolomics analysis.

claim: Lactate in RBCs negatively correlates with pathological RBC shapes, in contrast with the positive correlation in plasma.
source: Negative correlations result with lactate, in contrast with the positive correlation in plasma, and mannitol, for which decreased levels are associated with reduced deformability of RBCs (Burke et al., 1981).
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: Mannitol in RBCs negatively correlates with pathological shapes, and decreased levels are associated with reduced deformability of RBCs.
source: Negative correlations result with lactate, in contrast with the positive correlation in plasma, and mannitol, for which decreased levels are associated with reduced deformability of RBCs (Burke et al., 1981).
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis, with the deformability association cited from literature.

claim: ALB in RBCs negatively correlates with pathological shapes and is known to re-establish RBC discocyte shape in stored blood.
source: Among the proteins is ALB, known to re-establish RBC discocyte shape in stored blood (Reinhart et al., 2015) and TF, which is reduced in COVID-19 plasma and is correlated with increased levels of CRP and IL-6 (Claise et al., 2022, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis, with the ALB function cited from literature.

claim: TF in RBCs negatively correlates with pathological shapes, is reduced in COVID-19 plasma, and is correlated with increased levels of CRP and IL-6.
source: Among the proteins is ALB, known to re-establish RBC discocyte shape in stored blood (Reinhart et al., 2015) and TF, which is reduced in COVID-19 plasma and is correlated with increased levels of CRP and IL-6 (Claise et al., 2022, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis and cited literature.

claim: Tryptophan and related metabolites formyl-kynurenine, kynurenine and serotonin negatively correlate with pathological RBC shapes.
source: Tryptophan and the related metabolites formyl-kynurenine, kynurenine and serotonin negatively correlate with pathological RBC shapes, coherently with lower levels seen in patient RBCs (formyl-kynurenine, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: Serotonin and dopamine negatively correlate with the fraction of pathological RBC shapes.
source: Serotonin and dopamine result negatively correlated with the fraction of pathological RBC shapes.
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: Positive correlations exist between pathological RBC shapes and several amino acids, such as methionine, tyrosine, lysine, histidine, threonine, and arginine catabolism products.
source: In contrast, positive correlations exist with several amino acids, such as methionine, tyrosine, lysine, histidine, threonine, and arginine catabolism products through the urea cycle, specifically citrulline, ornithine, arginine-succinate and urate.
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: Creatine and creatinine levels positively correlate with pathological RBC shapes, suggesting enhanced arginine catabolism.
source: Creatine and creatinine levels also result positively correlated, further suggesting an enhanced arginine catabolism.
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis with an inference about arginine catabolism.

claim: RBC buffering activity to contrast altered amino acid metabolism implies their morphological impairment.
source: These results highlight that RBC buffering activity to contrast the altered amino acid metabolism implies their morphological impairment.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between amino acid changes and morphological impairment.

claim: Formyl-kynurenine and kynurenine negatively correlate with pathological RBC shapes, while positive correlations exist with anthranilate and picolinic acid, suggesting the ability of pathological RBCs to buffer kynurenine pathway metabolites.
source: Finally, while formyl-kynurenine and kynurenine negatively correlate, positive correlations exist with anthranilate and picolinic acid, suggesting the ability of pathological RBCs to buffer kynurenine pathway metabolites.
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis with an inference about buffering capacity.

claim: Gas and ion transport-related proteins, such as carbonic anhydrase (CA2) and band3 (SLC4A1), are linked to pathological RBC shapes.
source: Gas and ion transport-related proteins, such as carbonic anhydrase (CA2) and band3 (SLC4A1) are linked to pathological RBC shapes; a special highlight is a correlation with the expression of hemoglobin F subunits (HBG1 and HBG2).
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: A correlation exists between pathological RBC shapes and the expression of hemoglobin F subunits (HBG1 and HBG2).
source: Gas and ion transport-related proteins, such as carbonic anhydrase (CA2) and band3 (SLC4A1) are linked to pathological RBC shapes; a special highlight is a correlation with the expression of hemoglobin F subunits (HBG1 and HBG2).
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: The correlation with gas and ion transport proteins suggests a need to adjust oxygen transport, transporter activity, and pH buffering during the infection state.
source: These data suggest a need to adjust oxygen transport, transporter activity, and pH buffering (chloride/bicarbonate ratios impact intracellular pH of RBCs) during the infection state (Nemkov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation data, with a citation to support the pH buffering mechanism.

claim: Correlations are found between pathological RBC shapes and several proteasome-linked proteins with ATP-dependent function, indicating high levels of protein degradation and regulation of amino acid metabolism.
source: Other correlations are found with several proteasome-linked proteins, such as PSMB2, PSMB6, PSMA1, PSMC4, PSMC2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) with an ATP-dependent function, indicating high levels of protein degradation and regulation of amino acid metabolism in pathological RBCs.
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis with an inference about protein degradation.

claim: Enhanced antioxidant activity in pathological RBCs is indicated by positive correlations with glutathione metabolism-related enzymes.
source: Indications of an enhanced antioxidant activity to cope with increased oxidative stress in such cells is highlighted by positive correlations with glutathione metabolism-related enzymes, such as glutathione S-transferase Mu 3 (GSTM3), glutathione reductase (GSR), which maintains reduced glutathione, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the rate-limiting enzyme for the pentose-phosphate pathway (PPP), which is the only source for NADPH generation in RBCs, thus the main pathway for protection against oxidative stress.
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis with an inference about antioxidant activity.

claim: G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme for the pentose-phosphate pathway (PPP), which is the only source for NADPH generation in RBCs and the main pathway for protection against oxidative stress.
source: Indications of an enhanced antioxidant activity to cope with increased oxidative stress in such cells is highlighted by positive correlations with glutathione metabolism-related enzymes, such as glutathione S-transferase Mu 3 (GSTM3), glutathione reductase (GSR), which maintains reduced glutathione, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the rate-limiting enzyme for the pentose-phosphate pathway (PPP), which is the only source for NADPH generation in RBCs, thus the main pathway for protection against oxidative stress.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about RBC metabolism.

claim: A positive correlation exists between pathological RBC shapes and peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1) that catalyzes the reduction of hydrogen peroxide.
source: In addition, a positive correlation exists with peroxiredoxin 1 (PRDX1) that catalyzes the reduction of hydrogen peroxide.
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis.

claim: Correlations are found between pathological RBC shapes and nicotinamide-phosphoribosyl transferase (NAMPT), which catalyzes the biosynthesis of NAD.
source: Further correlations are found with nicotinamide-phosphoribosyl transferase (NAMPT), which catalyzes the biosynthesis of NAD, and NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase 3 (CYB5R3), which reduces methemoglobin, the oxidated form of hemoglobin to the ferric state.
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis.

claim: Correlations are found between pathological RBC shapes and NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase 3 (CYB5R3), which reduces methemoglobin.
source: Further correlations are found with nicotinamide-phosphoribosyl transferase (NAMPT), which catalyzes the biosynthesis of NAD, and NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase 3 (CYB5R3), which reduces methemoglobin, the oxidated form of hemoglobin to the ferric state.
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis.

claim: Morphological impairments observed in RBCs flowing in COVID-19 patient plasma are strongly related to markers of inflammation, oxidation, and hypoxia, which are associated with increased mortality risk.
source: Together, these data show that morphological impairments observed in RBCs flowing in COVID-19 patient plasma are strongly related to markers of inflammation, oxidation, and hypoxia, which are associated with increased mortality risk (D'Alessandro et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the correlation analysis results, with citation to support the mortality risk association.

claim: Microfluidic analysis demonstrates a significantly increased number of pathological RBC shapes, such as sphero-echinocytes, in the capillary flow of COVID-19 patients (PinP).
source: Our microfluidic analysis demonstrates a significantly increased number of pathological RBC shapes, such as sphero-echinocytes in the capillary flow of COVID-19 patients (PinP) (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the microfluidic experiments.

claim: Pathological RBC shape changes lead to an alteration of the microscale flow behavior since these RBCs are not able to adapt their shape to the imposed flow conditions compared to healthy controls.
source: These changes lead to an alteration of the microscale flow behavior since these RBCs are not able to adapt their shape to the imposed flow conditions compared to healthy controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in the microfluidic flow analysis.

claim: Although patients show increased levels of fibrinogen, which would favor enhanced formation of RBC clusters, their RBCs do not aggregate into rouleaux but form disorganized structures.
source: Although patients show increased levels of fibrinogen (Figure 1—source data 1), which would favor an enhanced formation of RBC clusters (Dasanna et al., 2022), their RBCs do not aggregate into rouleaux but form disorganized structures.
evidence: This is observed in the static images and supported by the fibrinogen data and citation.

claim: The severe alterations of RBC shapes and deformability hinder the formation of RBC aggregates in stasis.
source: Hence, we hypothesize that the severe alterations of RBC shapes and deformability hinder the formation of RBC aggregates in stasis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed data.

claim: COVID-19 RBCs are able to revert their shape to biconcave disks in stasis and healthy croissant and slipper shapes in flow, resulting in single-cell flow behavior comparable to control samples.
source: However, COVID-19 RBCs are able to revert their shape to biconcave disks in stasis and healthy croissant and slipper shapes in flow, resulting in a single-cell flow behavior comparable to control samples.
evidence: This is observed in the plasma exchange experiments.

claim: The reversibility of sphero-echinocytes contradicts previous literature.
source: Interestingly, the reversibility of sphero-echinocytes contradicts previous literature.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding relative to prior beliefs.

claim: It was previously assumed that sphero-echinocytes cannot reverse to discocytes due to membrane loss through vesiculation that imbalances the structure of the lipid bilayer, but this was not demonstrated mathematically.
source: Up to now, it was assumed that sphero-echinocytes cannot reverse to discocytes due to membrane loss through vesiculation that imbalances the structure of the lipid bilayer but this was not demonstrated mathematically (Lim H. W. et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about prior assumptions in the field, with citation.

claim: Marcel Bessis declared in his book 'Red Cell Shape' that sphero-echinocytes are not reversible to discocytes, without providing experimental proof.
source: Marcel Bessis, one of the fathers of RBC classification based on their morphology, declared in his book 'Red Cell Shape' (Bessis et al., 1973) that sphero-echinocytes are not reversible to discocytes, without providing an experimental proof.
evidence: This is a historical statement about prior beliefs, with citation.

claim: In previous work, spherocytes were described to be able to revert to biconcave disks as long as they have not reached the stage of prolytic spheres.
source: However, in previous work (Ponder, 1948), spherocytes, the very last transition stage of RBC before hemolysis, were described to be able to revert to biconcave disks as long as they have not reached the stage of prolytic spheres (Ponder, 1948).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ponder, 1948.

claim: Morphological alterations concomitant to membrane shedding and acquisition of a spheroechinocytic phenotype, though apparently reversible, would still give rise to smaller RBCs of decreased volumes, which are preferentially cleared from the bloodstream via splenic sequestration.
source: Moreover, it has been recently shown that morphological alterations concomitant to membrane shedding and acquisition of a spheroechinocytic phenotype, though apparently reversible in the present study, would still give rise to smaller RBCs of decreased volumes, which are preferentially cleared from the bloodstream via splenic sequestration (Roussel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roussel et al., 2021.

claim: Echinocytes presence is not a specific feature of COVID-19 infection but has been previously observed in stasis in blood smears of septic patients.
source: Of note, echinocytes presence is not a specific feature of COVID-19 infection but has been previously observed in stasis in blood smears of septic patients (Bateman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bateman et al., 2017.

claim: Patient plasma results in increased levels of inflammation and hypercoagulation markers, in accordance with previously published data.
source: Patient plasma results in increased levels of inflammation and hypercoagulation markers, in accordance with previously published data (Thomas et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is from the proteomics analysis, with citation to prior work.

claim: Kynurenine levels are associated with hypoxia markers and interferon signaling (IFNG).
source: Kynurenine levels are associated with hypoxia markers and interferon signaling (IFNG) (D'Alessandro et al., 2021b; Galbraith et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The restoration of proteins and metabolites levels is acute and immediate and occurs at the expense of RBC shapes.
source: The restoration of proteins and metabolites levels is acute and immediate and occurs at the expense of RBC shapes.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid changes observed in the omics data after plasma exchange.

claim: The obtained results highlight a non-previously identified 'sponge-like' behavior of RBCs that is used to control plasma homeostasis.
source: The obtained results highlight a non-previously identified 'sponge-like' behavior of RBCs that is used to control plasma homeostasis.
evidence: This is a novel interpretation of the data showing RBC buffering capacity.

claim: These influences and adaptations to the surrounding environment may be a specific feature of RBCs since they cannot synthesize new proteins and thus respond to needs through metabolic adjustments that also involve shape transformations.
source: These influences and adaptations to the surrounding environment may be a specific feature of RBCs since they cannot synthesize new proteins and thus respond to needs through metabolic adjustments that also involve shape transformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed metabolic changes and the known biology of RBCs.

claim: Proteomics and metabolomics data on RBCs confirm that the differences between healthy and patient cells reflect the differences observed in their plasma content.
source: Proteomics and metabolomics data on RBCs indeed confirm that the differences between healthy and patient cells reflect the differences observed in their plasma content.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the omics data from RBCs and plasma.

claim: Morphologically impaired COVID-19 RBCs are associated with markers of inflammation, oxidation, and hypoxia in the plasma.
source: A deeper investigation on morphologically impaired COVID-19 RBCs by correlation analysis results in their association with markers of inflammation, oxidation, and hypoxia in the plasma, features that act in a tight relation to overcome the infection.
evidence: This is from the Spearman correlation analysis.

claim: Guanidinoacetate and ornithine correlations in patient RBCs suggest more activity of arginase that results in creatine production, which is used for ATP synthesis.
source: Guanidinoacetate and ornithine correlations in patient RBCs suggest more activity of arginase that results in creatine production, which is used for ATP synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolomics data and known metabolic pathways.

claim: Incubation of RBCs with arginine leads to the production of citrulline, ornithine, and urea, indicating an RBC-related enzymatic machinery for arginine metabolism.
source: It was previously seen that incubation of RBCs with arginine leads to the production of citrulline, ornithine, and urea, indicating an RBC-related enzymatic machinery for arginine metabolism (Ramírez-Zamora et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ramírez-Zamora et al., 2013.

claim: The functional role of increased arginine catabolism may be to increase nitric oxide (NO) availability to respond to hypoxia, inducing vasodilation for increased blood flow.
source: The functional role of increased arginine catabolism may be to increase nitric oxide (NO) availability to respond to hypoxia, inducing vasodilation for an increased blood flow.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the metabolic changes.

claim: Arginine supplementation increases T-cell proliferation and macrophage activity, thus it could contribute to enhance immune response.
source: Arginine supplementation increases T-cell proliferation and macrophage activity, thus it could contribute to enhance immune response (D'Alessandro et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to D'Alessandro et al., 2021b.

claim: Creatine leads to ATP synthesis, which increases during the immune response to boost leukocyte proliferation and activity.
source: As well, creatine leads to ATP synthesis, which increases during the immune response to boost leukocyte proliferation and activity.
evidence: This is based on known metabolic pathways and immune cell biology.

claim: Tryptophan metabolism is involved in nicotinamide and NAD production.
source: Moreover, tryptophan metabolism is involved in nicotinamide and NAD production.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: NAD formation from tryptophan metabolism was demonstrated to boost macrophage phagocytic activity during immune response.
source: NAD is implicated in the glycolytic pathway and oxidative phosphorylation and its formation from tryptophan metabolism was demonstrated to boost macrophage phagocytic activity during immune response (Minhas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Minhas et al., 2019.

claim: Dopamine has a role in the initiation of immune responses in lymphocytes.
source: Dopamine has a role in the initiation of immune responses in lymphocytes (Buttarelli et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buttarelli et al., 2011.

claim: The biosynthesis of serotonin and dopamine is thought to decrease in COVID-19 infection due to a co-expression and functional link with ACE2.
source: The biosynthesis of serotonin and dopamine, which are negatively correlated with morphological RBC deviations, is thought to decrease in COVID-19 infection due to a co-expression and a functional link with Angiotensin I Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) (Nataf, 2020), the main receptor for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nataf, 2020.

claim: ACE2 is the main receptor for SARS-CoV-2.
source: The biosynthesis of serotonin and dopamine, which are negatively correlated with morphological RBC deviations, is thought to decrease in COVID-19 infection due to a co-expression and a functional link with Angiotensin I Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) (Nataf, 2020), the main receptor for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 entry.

claim: The data highlight the relevance of RBC buffering effect for immune cell activity regulation.
source: Together, these data highlight the relevance of RBC buffering effect for immune cell activity regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic changes and their potential immune implications.

claim: Positive correlations with plasma lactate levels are linked to increased energy demand.
source: Positive correlations with plasma lactate levels are also linked to increased energy demand.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation data and known metabolic pathways.

claim: Hypoxia causes a boost in glycolysis to produce and release more ATP that stimulates NO production and vasodilation, as well as 2,3-DPG that increases deoxyhemoglobin release of oxygen.
source: Hypoxia causes a boost in glycolysis to produce and release more ATP that stimulates NO production and vasodilation, as well as 2,3-DPG that increases deoxyhemoglobin release of oxygen (Nemkov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nemkov et al., 2018.

claim: ATP release results in increased adenosine and xanthine in hypoxic plasma.
source: ATP release also results in increased adenosine and xanthine in hypoxic plasma, as observed in our data.
evidence: This is observed in the metabolomics data and linked to known hypoxia responses.

claim: Adenosine levels remain high because PKA triggers a hypoxia-induced proteasome that degrades adenosine transporters.
source: Adenosine levels remain high because PKA triggers a hypoxia-induced proteasome that degrades adenosine transporters (Nemkov et al., 2018), as we show from the correlation with several proteasome ATP-dependent proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nemkov et al., 2018 and the proteomics data.

claim: More glycolysis results in less PPP for glutathione reduction, so less NADPH formation and presumably less antioxidant capacity of RBCs.
source: More glycolysis results in less PPP for glutathione reduction, so less NADPH formation and presumably less antioxidant capacity of RBCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic data and known metabolic pathways.

claim: The oxygen dissociation curve was not found different in COVID-19 patients.
source: Although the oxygen dissociation curve was not found different in COVID-19 patients (Böning et al., 2021) the presence of markers of hypoxia is expectable, considering that COVID-19 infection often results in lowered blood oxygen saturation, and in ECMO patients it is reduced until 82% (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Böning et al., 2021.

claim: COVID-19 infection often results in lowered blood oxygen saturation, and in ECMO patients it is reduced until 82%.
source: Although the oxygen dissociation curve was not found different in COVID-19 patients (Böning et al., 2021) the presence of markers of hypoxia is expectable, considering that COVID-19 infection often results in lowered blood oxygen saturation, and in ECMO patients it is reduced until 82% (Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2013.

claim: A reason for no differences in the oxygen dissociation curve may be due to methemoglobin, which increases hemoglobin oxygen affinity and may compensate the opposite effect of 2,3-DPG.
source: A reason for no differences in the oxygen dissociation curve may be due to methemoglobin, which increases hemoglobin oxygen affinity and may compensate the opposite effect of 2,3-DPG (Böning et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to Böning et al., 2021.

claim: Positive correlations are found with methemoglobin and hemoglobin F globin chains, whose expression is stimulated by hypoxia.
source: Indeed, we found positive correlations with methemoglobin and hemoglobin F globin chains, whose expression is stimulated by hypoxia (Simionato et al., 2022).
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis, with citation to support the hypoxia-stimulated expression.

claim: The correlation data highlight an effect of the infectious state also at the level of erythropoiesis.
source: This highlights an effect of the infectious state also at the level of erythropoiesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the hemoglobin F expression data.

claim: Sphero-echinocytes show increased antioxidant activity since they are positively correlated with GSR, G6PD, and PRDX1.
source: Sphero-echinocytes show increased antioxidant activity since they are positively correlated with GSR, which catalyzes glutathione reduction, G6PD that is necessary for NADPH formation, and PRDX1, which reduces hydroperoxides.
evidence: This is from the correlation analysis.

claim: The increased antioxidant response is associated with the infectious state since in septic patients proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF alpha promote ROS generation to destroy bacteria.
source: This response is associated with the infectious state since in septic patients proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF alpha promote ROS generation to destroy bacteria (Bateman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bateman et al., 2017.

claim: Oxidation of band 3, spectrin (SPTA1) and ankyrin (ANK1) has been reported in COVID-19 RBCs.
source: We could not find differences in, for example, levels of band 3 (AE1), to indicate oxidative stress-associated loss of cytoskeletal proteins, but it was reported oxidation of band 3, spectrin (SPTA1) and ankyrin (ANK1) (Thomas et al., 2020a), which, along with alterations of the lipid compartments, may alter RBC deformability.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2020a.

claim: Oxidation of cytoskeletal proteins, along with alterations of the lipid compartments, may alter RBC deformability.
source: We could not find differences in, for example, levels of band 3 (AE1), to indicate oxidative stress-associated loss of cytoskeletal proteins, but it was reported oxidation of band 3, spectrin (SPTA1) and ankyrin (ANK1) (Thomas et al., 2020a), which, along with alterations of the lipid compartments, may alter RBC deformability.
evidence: This is inferred from cited literature and known RBC biology.

claim: The impaired deformability in COVID-19 cells is mostly reversible, thus not indicating damaged antioxidant mechanisms in RBCs.
source: We see that the impaired deformability in COVID-19 cells is mostly reversible, thus not indicating damaged antioxidant mechanisms in RBCs, but rather increased oxidative stress caused by higher ROS generation during the infection that may be resolved by increasing RBC antioxidant defense.
evidence: This is inferred from the reversibility observed in the plasma exchange experiments.

claim: Increased oxidative stress is caused by higher ROS generation during the infection that may be resolved by increasing RBC antioxidant defense.
source: We see that the impaired deformability in COVID-19 cells is mostly reversible, thus not indicating damaged antioxidant mechanisms in RBCs, but rather increased oxidative stress caused by higher ROS generation during the infection that may be resolved by increasing RBC antioxidant defense.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reversibility and increased antioxidant enzyme expression.

claim: Convalescent plasma transfusion was shown not to be associated with improved clinical outcomes.
source: The results of our study create the basis for possible clinical impacts: convalescent plasma transfusion was shown not to be associated with improved clinical outcomes (Janiaud et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Janiaud et al., 2021.

claim: Plasma transfusions from healthy individuals may benefit RBC flow properties in COVID-19 patients that may potentially decrease RBC-related thrombotic risk.
source: While plasma transfusions from healthy individuals may benefit RBC flow properties in COVID-19 patients that may potentially decrease RBC-related thrombotic risk (Byrnes and Wolberg, 2017), patient antibodies would be diluted, possibly compromising the efficacy of the immune response to the virus.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings, with citation to support the thrombotic risk concept.

claim: Plasma transfusions from healthy individuals would dilute patient antibodies, possibly compromising the efficacy of the immune response to the virus.
source: While plasma transfusions from healthy individuals may benefit RBC flow properties in COVID-19 patients that may potentially decrease RBC-related thrombotic risk (Byrnes and Wolberg, 2017), patient antibodies would be diluted, possibly compromising the efficacy of the immune response to the virus.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of plasma transfusion.

claim: It is unclear whether a plasma or erythrocyte concentrate (EC) transfusion will be beneficial for COVID-19 patients.
source: Although the observed severe changes in RBC shapes could potentially act as a starting point for clinical studies, it is unclear whether a plasma or erythrocyte concentrate (EC) transfusion will be beneficial.
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty regarding clinical applications.

claim: Further studies are necessary to evaluate the mechanisms through which RBCs re-establish plasma equilibria, potentially decreasing patient mortality risk.
source: Therefore, further studies are necessary to evaluate the mechanisms through which RBCs re-establish plasma equilibria, potentially decreasing patient mortality risk.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Blood was drawn from five healthy volunteers and 14 COVID-19 patients admitted at the ICU at the Frankfurt University Hospital.
source: Nine mL of blood is drawn in heparin tubes from five healthy volunteers under informed consent and 14 COVID-19 patients admitted at the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) at the Frankfurt University Hospital, seven of which with supported ventilation and six receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the study sample collection.

claim: Seven COVID-19 patients had supported ventilation and six were receiving ECMO.
source: Nine mL of blood is drawn in heparin tubes from five healthy volunteers under informed consent and 14 COVID-19 patients admitted at the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) at the Frankfurt University Hospital, seven of which with supported ventilation and six receiving extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) (Figure 1—source data 1).
